craft_claim: Juvenal's Satires supply the indignation register of the cynical voice — moralized, controlled rage at vice stated in terms of violated standards — distinct from Horatian amusement; borrowed into prose it is the tone's high, accusatory register.

supporting_evidence.note: The commentary documents the invective mode of Satire 1: a speaker cataloguing Roman vices in a moralized, indignant key, with outrage organized as argument rather than as raw complaint.

supporting_evidence.location: Loeb LCL 91, introduction and the Satires (Books 1-5)
supporting_evidence.note: The standard facing-page edition establishes the Satires' moralizing, accusatory register as the collection's organizing stance; this is the locating text for the mode cited here.

supporting_evidence.location: Entries on satire and satirical modes
supporting_evidence.note: Reference entries distinguish Juvenalian satire (provocative moral indictment) from Horatian (gentle, amused correction) and Menippean (structural assault on systems), fixing the vocabulary the tone borrows.
The Satires perform the mode itself: indignation sustained across books by catalogue, apostrophe, and the consistency of a speaker who expects better of Rome and gets none.

counterevidence.note: Modern commentary reads the satirist's fury as a constructed speakerly persona; indignant directness belongs to a voice the poet assigns, which cautions against reading Juvenalian rage as unmasked authorial opinion.

scope: The high register of the cynical voice; also the tonal seam where the tone meets the satirical genre's target-prosecuting engine.
exceptions: Borrowed without a target, Juvenalian indignation degenerates into generalized misanthropy (see the failure claim).
Horatian and Menippean registers are alternative satirical voices the cynical tone can wear when indictment would be overkill.
